passages.t: ‘It is for freedom that Christ has set us free’
passages.happening:
“It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery” (verse 1).

Then Paul speaks as plainly as he can. “Take notice: I, Paul, tell you that if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all” (verse 2). A man who is circumcised for this reason is “obligated to obey the whole law” (verse 3). “You who are trying to be justified by the law have been severed from Christ; you have fallen away from grace” (verse 4).

“But by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness” (verse 5). “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value. All that matters is faith, expressed through love” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
A yoke was the wooden frame laid on the necks of oxen so that they could pull a load. It was a common picture of being under someone's power. Jewish teachers could speak well of ‘the yoke of the law’, a willing service to God, and Jesus called his own yoke easy (Matthew 11:29-30). Peter, speaking of Gentile believers, called the law “a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear” (Acts 15:10). Paul says that for Gentiles already free in Christ, taking on the law as the price of belonging would be a yoke of slavery.

Verse 2 does not say that circumcision itself is evil. Paul's own helper Timothy, whose mother was Jewish, was circumcised (Acts 16:3). Verse 6 says plainly that circumcision, in itself, means nothing either way. The danger is being circumcised in order to be justified, to stand right with God. That means trusting in something besides Christ. And if you trust in the law for your standing, you must keep the whole of it.

‘Severed from Christ’ and ‘fallen away from grace’ are strong words. Paul is saying that the two ways cannot be mixed. You cannot stand on grace and on your own record at the same time. To choose the law as the way to be right with God is to step off the ground of grace.

Verse 6 is one of Paul's great summaries. What counts is not a mark on the body but ‘faith, expressed through love’. Faith is not idle. It works, and the way it works is love.
passages.ot:
The prophets had long said that what God wanted was a changed heart, not only a mark on the body. Moses promised, “The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts and the hearts of your descendants, and you will love Him with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 30:6). Jeremiah called out, “Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and remove the foreskins of your hearts” (Jeremiah 4:4).

Paul's ‘faith, expressed through love’ stands in that line. The question was never only the body, but the heart turned to God in trust and love.
passages.hard:
‘You have fallen away from grace’ (verse 4). Can a believer lose salvation?

First, notice what Paul is talking about. He is not speaking of believers who sin and repent. He is speaking of people who were turning from grace to the law as the way to stand right with God. ‘Falling from grace’ here means falling into law, trading the gift for wages.

Christians then read the warning in different ways. Much of the Reformed and Baptist world holds that those truly saved are kept by God and cannot finally be lost. They read verse 4 as a real and serious warning, which God uses to keep his people, and they hold that those who finally turn away show they never truly belonged. Much of the Wesleyan, Arminian and Catholic world holds that a person can turn away and forfeit salvation, and they read verse 4 more directly. These notes do not choose. The site's note on Romans 8:31-39 sets out both, and so does the Honest Answer, ‘Can you lose your salvation?’

Notice too that Paul still calls the Galatians ‘brothers’, and says in verse 10, “I am confident in the Lord that you will take no other view”. The warning is meant to bring them home, not to drive them to despair.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul says that what matters is ‘faith, expressed through love’. Ask what your faith is expressed through: knowledge, habits, opinions, or love. And ask whether there is any yoke you have picked up again, a way of trying to earn what Christ has already given. Paul says, ‘Stand firm’.

passages.happening:
“You were running so well. Who has obstructed you from obeying the truth?” (verse 7). This way of thinking does not come from God, who called them (verse 8). “A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough” (verse 9).

Paul is still hopeful. “I am confident in the Lord that you will take no other view” (verse 10). Whoever is troubling them will answer to God.

Some were saying that Paul himself still preached circumcision. He answers, “Now, brothers, if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been abolished” (verse 11).

Then his angriest sentence: “As for those who are agitating you, I wish they would proceed to emasculate themselves!” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
‘Running’ is a picture from the races. The word for ‘obstructed’ may picture someone cutting in on a runner and breaking his stride.

Leaven was a lump of old, fermented dough kept back from the last baking and mixed into new dough to make it rise. A little spread through the whole lump. At Passover, Israel cleared all leaven from their homes, and so leaven became a picture of something that spreads and corrupts. Paul means that a small change to the gospel does not stay small.

Verse 11 shows a rumour about Paul. Perhaps people pointed out that he lived as a Jew among Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20), or that he had Timothy circumcised. Paul answers that if he preached circumcision as the way into God's people, no one would persecute him. The cross offends because it says that nothing we add can save us.

Verse 12 is a bitter joke. Circumcision cuts the body. Paul wishes the teachers who are so keen on cutting would go further and castrate themselves. Some readers think the Galatians would have thought at once of the priests of the goddess Cybele, whose chief shrine was at Pessinus in Galatia, and who castrated themselves in her worship. Others doubt that Paul had them in mind. Either way, the jab is sharp. Under the law, such a man could not enter the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:1).
passages.ot:
Israel removed leaven at Passover: “On the first day you are to remove the leaven from your houses” (Exodus 12:15). Paul uses the same picture in 1 Corinthians 5:6-8.

The law kept a castrated man out of Israel's assembly: “No man with crushed or severed genitals may enter the assembly of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 23:1). But the prophets looked ahead to a day of welcome. Isaiah heard God say to eunuchs who hold fast to his covenant, “I will give them, in My house and within My walls, a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5). In Acts, an Ethiopian eunuch is one of the first to be baptized (Acts 8:38).
passages.hard:
What should we make of verse 12?

It is the harshest thing Paul ever wrote, and these notes will not pretend otherwise. It shows his anger at people who, in his judgment, were harming young believers and twisting the gospel. Anger at harm done to the weak is not always wrong.

But the verse is not a pattern for how believers speak to or about anyone. Paul himself, in this same chapter, warns against “biting and devouring one another” (verse 15), and names “rage” and “hatred” among the works of the flesh (verse 20). The Bible records his outburst honestly, as it records the angry psalms, without telling us to copy it. Paul's own rule is to speak the truth in love, and in the next chapter he tells believers to restore one who falls “with a spirit of gentleness” (6:1).

Notice also that the prophets promised welcome for eunuchs who love God (Isaiah 56:3-5). Paul's joke is aimed at the teachers' message, not at anyone's body.
passages.asks: A little leaven works through the whole batch. Ask what small additions to the gospel you have let in without noticing: a little pride, a little earning, a little fear of others. And when you are angry at real harm, ask how to let that anger serve truth and protection, without letting it turn into contempt.

passages.t: Free to serve one another in love
passages.happening:
“For you, brothers, were called to freedom; but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. Rather, serve one another in love” (verse 13).

“The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself’” (verse 14).

“But if you keep on biting and devouring one another, watch out, or you will be consumed by one another” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Paul has argued hard for freedom. Now he guards it from a misunderstanding. Someone might say: if I am not under the law, I can do as I please. Paul says no.

‘Opportunity’ was a word for a base of operations, a foothold from which an army launches an attack. Freedom must not become a foothold for the flesh, the self turned in on itself.

Then a surprise. ‘Serve’ is the verb for working as a slave. Paul has just said the Galatians must not go back to slavery. Now he says they should be slaves to one another, in love. Christian freedom is not freedom from others. It is freedom for them.

Verse 14 shows that Paul is not against the law's purpose. The whole law is fulfilled in love. What the law aimed at, the Spirit now brings about.

Verse 15 hints that the churches in Galatia were already quarrelling. ‘Biting and devouring’ is the language of wild animals. A church that fights over who is truly faithful can end up destroying itself.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes Leviticus: “Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD” (Leviticus 19:18). Jesus also named this as one of the two great commandments (Mark 12:31).

The prophets summed up the law in the same spirit: “He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8).
passages.asks: Paul says freedom is for serving one another. Ask what you think your freedom in Christ is for. And ask whether there is anyone in your church you have been biting at, in word or in your heart. Love your neighbour as yourself is not the easy part of the law. It is the whole of it.

passages.happening:
“So I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh” (verse 16). The flesh and the Spirit want opposite things, “so that you do not do what you want” (verse 17). “But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law” (verse 18).

Then Paul lists what the flesh produces. “The acts of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity, and debauchery; idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions, and envy; drunkenness, orgies, and the like” (verses 19-21).

“I warn you, as I did before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
‘Walk by the Spirit’ means to live day by day in step with God's Spirit, the way you walk beside a friend.

‘Flesh’ in Paul does not mean the body as bad. God made the body, and Christ took a human body. ‘Flesh’ here means human life turned away from God and in on itself. It can show itself in obvious sins, and it can also show itself in religious pride.

Look at the list. It begins with sins of sex and of false worship, which Gentile hearers knew well from the life of their cities. ‘Sorcery’ is the word for using drugs and spells in magic. But most of the list is about how people treat one another: hatred, discord, jealousy, rage, rivalries, divisions, factions, envy. Eight of the fifteen are sins that tear a community apart. Those are just the sins a church quarrelling over the law might fall into.

Ancient moral teachers often made lists of vices and virtues. Paul uses the familiar form but roots it in the Spirit, not in human effort.

‘Those who practice such things’ speaks of a way of life, a settled path, not a single fall.
passages.ot:
The prophets promised that God's Spirit would do what the law could not. “I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes and to carefully observe My ordinances” (Ezekiel 36:27). And through Jeremiah, God promised to write his law on hearts: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33).

The struggle between what is right and what we want is old. Cain was warned, “sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it” (Genesis 4:7).
passages.hard:
‘Those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God’ (verse 21). Does this mean a Christian who falls into one of these sins is lost?

Paul speaks of those who ‘practice’ these things, a way of life chosen and held to, not a believer who stumbles and turns back. In another letter, after a similar list, he says, “And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified” (1 Corinthians 6:11). The list is a warning about where a life lived for the flesh leads, and a call to turn. It is not a door slammed on those who repent.

Christians differ on whether a true believer can finally fall away, as the note on verses 1 to 6 sets out. They agree that this warning is serious, and that God's mercy is wide open to anyone who turns to him.

If you are worn down by failing again and again, or caught in an addiction you cannot break, you are not alone, and you are not beyond help. Please talk to someone: a doctor, a pastor, a counsellor, or a group that helps people with what you are facing. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Most of Paul's list is about how people treat one another. Ask which of these you find easiest to excuse in yourself: rivalry, envy, anger, taking sides. Then ask what it would look like to walk by the Spirit in the place where you most often fall.

passages.happening:
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law” (verses 22-23).

“Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (verse 24). “Since we live by the Spirit, let us walk in step with the Spirit” (verse 25).

“Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying one another” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Notice the word ‘fruit’, singular. The flesh produces many separate works. The Spirit grows one harvest with many sides. These nine are not a list of separate achievements to tick off. They are one life, the life of Christ, growing in a person.

Fruit is not made; it grows. A farmer cannot force an apple. He plants, waters and waits. Paul is saying that these qualities come from the Spirit's life within, not from trying harder.

‘Against such things there is no law’ is a quiet joke. No law has ever been passed against kindness. The law was never needed to stop people from loving too much.

‘Crucified the flesh’ looks back to 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ”. The old self has been put to death with Christ. Believers still feel its pull, but it is not their master.

‘Walk in step with’ was used of soldiers marching in line, or of keeping in line with a rule. The Spirit sets the pace, and believers keep step.

Verse 26 brings it back to the churches. Even talk of the Spirit can become a reason to feel superior. Paul says: no conceit, no provoking, no envy.
passages.ot:
The Psalms describe the righteous person as a fruitful tree: “He is like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season, whose leaf does not wither” (Psalm 1:3).

Isaiah promised that the land itself would change, waiting “until the Spirit is poured out upon us from on high. Then the desert will be an orchard” (Isaiah 32:15). And the harvest will be peace: “The work of righteousness will be peace” (Isaiah 32:17).

Several of the nine are what the Old Testament says of God himself. He is “slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). The fruit of the Spirit is God's own character growing in his people.
passages.asks: Read the nine slowly. Ask which of them you see growing in your life, and which seems barely planted. Then ask what helps fruit grow: not straining, but staying close to its source. What would it mean for you to keep in step with the Spirit this week?
